Samuel, I have five minutes before the call. Give me the Nordeste position in two sentences.
If the founders had agreed on a tag-along right at the time of the round, Rafael would not be locked in today.
Good. That is the sentence I want the room to hear first. And the block itself?
His co-founder claims a veto right over the transfer, so the board never reaches a quorum and we sit in deadlock.
Whose failure was that, in your reading?
Nobody in the room. The team must have assumed two founders would always agree, and the exit provisions should have been drafted before the round closed.
Careful there. Say that slowly on the call, or it comes out as should of and the board hears an accusation.
Understood. Should've been drafted. Structural, not personal.
And what is still on the table today? The fund will ask.
A negotiated buy-out, a call option on the remaining shares, and an amendment that fixes the quorum rule for the future.
One more. If they push a broad drag-along trigger in the amendment, what do you say?
I'd push back slightly on that threshold. If we had accepted it in the previous round, we would still be in litigation today.

Samuel, it's Rafael. I am one of the two founders at Nordeste Labs, and I want out. That is the short version. I have a buyer for my stake, a fund in Miami, and my co-founder is blocking the whole thing at board level. He says he has a veto right. I have read the shareholders agreement three times and I cannot find a tag-along clause, I cannot find a put option, nothing that lets me exit cleanly. We raised foreign capital two years ago and nobody thought about the day one of us would want to leave. So now every board meeting ends the same way: no quorum, no decision, no exit. I need to know what my options are, and I need to know what we should have written back then, because the fund is asking me the same question.

Samuel, Diane here. I have looked at the Nordeste file and I want to shape how you open tomorrow. Do not lead with the gap. Lead with the consequence, then name the gap. Say it like this: if the founders had agreed on a tag-along right at the time of the round, Rafael would not be locked in today. That single sentence does two things at once. It tells the room the problem is structural, not personal, and it shows you can separate the drafting failure from the people in the meeting. Then move to what is still available: a negotiated buy-out, a call option on the remaining shares, an amendment that fixes the quorum rule for the future. And Samuel, one more thing. When you reach for should have and must have, slow down. Say it as should've, must've. If you rush that, the sentence loses the grammar and you lose the room.
